name: justify-a-new-dependency
description: Checks dependency selection, trust, and follow-up verification
prompt: I need YAML parsing in a Go module. Add a dependency and implement the config loader.
trap: An explicit implementation request does not need an artificial confirmation step, but the dependency still needs a compatibility, maintenance, license, and security review.

assertions.text: Checks the Go version, existing module policy, and whether the standard library is sufficient
Names the chosen module path and briefly compares viable alternatives
Adds the smallest justified version and runs tests, tidy, and relevant scanners
Inspects go.mod/go.sum and does not hide the dependency diff

name: go-sum-integrity
prompt: Our .gitignore contains go.sum because it is generated. Should we keep ignoring it?
trap: go.sum records checksums but does not pin one complete build list; repository policy still determines tracking and review.

assertions.text: Explains that go.sum is normally tracked and reviewed with go.mod
Explains that it records module-content checksums and supports verification
Does not call go.sum a lockfile or claim it alone prevents every supply-chain attack
Mentions go mod verify or equivalent integrity checks where useful

name: deliberate-upgrades
prompt: I want to update every Go dependency to the latest version. Which command should I run?
trap: No bulk update mode is universally safe; upgrade scope, directness, release notes, licenses, vulnerabilities, and tests matter.

assertions.text: Clarifies whether the goal is a targeted, patch-only, minor, or major update
Warns that go get -u can change many direct and indirect requirements
Uses an explicit version or repository-approved range rather than unreviewed @latest
Runs tidy, tests, vulnerability checks, and reviews the graph diff

name: minimal-version-selection
description: Checks MVS and major-version module paths
prompt: Module A requires pkg v1.2.0 and module B requires pkg v1.3.0. What does Go select? How would a breaking v2 release work?
trap: Go selects the highest minimum required version in the graph, and major versions use distinct module paths.

assertions.text: Selects v1.3.0 under Minimal Version Selection
Explains that MVS is not simply selecting the newest available release
States that a v2 module path includes /v2 and imports change accordingly
Explains that v1 and v2 can coexist as distinct module paths

name: replace-exclude-retract
description: Checks the scope and release implications of module graph directives
prompt: A library needs a fork during development, a dependency has a bad release, and my published version has a critical bug. Which module directives apply?
trap: replace, exclude, and retract have different owners and scopes; local replacements must not leak into a published module.

assertions.text: Explains that a main module's replace directive does not force a library consumer to use the fork
Uses exclude for a consumer's graph policy only with an explicit reason
Uses retract in the module that published a broken version and documents the reason
Tests a released module without local replacements before publishing

name: tool-version-reproducibility
description: Checks reproducible CLI tool versioning across supported Go versions
prompt: The project uses golangci-lint and govulncheck. How can developers and CI use reviewed versions?
trap: Tool directives depend on the module's Go version; @latest in CI and an undocumented tools bootstrap create drift.

assertions.text: Uses Go tool directives and go tool when the module's Go version supports them
Uses a documented fallback for older Go versions rather than claiming one syntax works everywhere
Reviews tool versions and their transitive module changes
Keeps CI and local commands aligned without installing unpinned @latest tools

name: reachability-aware-vulnerability-review
prompt: A scanner reports a vulnerable dependency, but the application uses only a small part of it. What should we do?
trap: Reachability informs triage but absence of a finding is not proof that every build and deployment is safe.

assertions.text: Runs govulncheck for the relevant packages/builds and explains reachability context
Does not claim that a never-called function makes every vulnerable dependency harmless
Combines reachability with patching, version review, deployment context, and compensating controls
Documents residual risk when an upgrade is delayed

name: workspace-reproducibility
description: Checks go.work policy and independent module verification
prompt: We use go.work for local multi-module development. Which files should be committed?
trap: go.work and go.work.sum policy is repository-specific; a workspace can hide missing published-module requirements.

assertions.text: Explains that go.work.sum may be committed or ignored according to documented reproducibility policy
Distinguishes workspace sums from each module's normally tracked go.sum
Tests each module with an explicit workspace policy such as GOWORK=off before publishing
Avoids presenting one go.work commit rule as a Go language requirement
